fields.description:
The issue was initially reported as an unusually long load phase in py-tpcc workloads. The issue appears intermittently as a few inserts in the load phase will get stuck for more than a few hours. Related PERF and HELP tickets have more information on the history of the issue.

[~bruce.lucas] has come up with a standalone reproducer, attached to the ticket.

Issue:
When inserting into a unique index, there is potential to get stuck repeatedly searching history store, ie calling {{__wt_hs_find_upd}}. We see a very high {{history store table reads missed}} statistic in these runs, which convey that these searches through history store are not returning anything. A callgraph that reflects this situation:

!hs.png|width=600!

Observed behaviour with the repro script:
* Observed behaviour in 4.4 is that insert rate is erratic, and a couple of the threads typically seem to get stuck apparently indefinitely with a high rate of missed history store reads with stacks like the above.

Acceptance criterion:
* With the repro script: Expected behaviour (same as observed in 4.2) is that insert rate should be steady and each thread should complete at about the same time
* py-tpcc load phase should not get stuck

Note:

Is it possible that the unique index insertion code needs to be checked/optimized with history store searches? For a unique index, we insert and then immediately remove a prefix to prevent consecutive insertions from other transactions. Then we search for the existence of the actual index key for a duplicate check. It appears like that search after insertion/removal is somehow getting stuck in the history store.

[~haribabu.kommi], [~chenhao.qu], you both worked on this aspect of the code. Do you think we have seen similar issues in our testing or fixed anything recently? If not, consider picking this ticket in the next sprint, as getting it solved will resolve several perf issues.

I've got the reproducer running, I've cut it down significantly and it repro's once every 3 runs for me. I also briefly investigated differences between 4.4.0 and 4.4.2 however the changeset is quite large so I'm not going to continue down that road for now. 

I've added prints, and modified the checkpoint interval to be every 5 seconds. As such I can kill the mongodb instance as it is searching for the relevant history store record and dump the history store to disk and see what I find. 

With only 10 threads now and a significantly reduce data set I can see that occasionally one thread gets caught in this loop.

So I think I understand what is happening here, the process of creating a unique index entry for 50000 unique entries exposes a sort of history store edge case. Given the steps involved:
 # Insert prefix
 # Remove prefix
 # Search_near for prefix
 ## Prev -> next to the actual key

The insertion and removal occurring in the same txn results in an effectively invisible update, which is being done to guarantee that there aren't collisions. Our search near however has to traverse 10000 invisible prefix updates. Now this is fine while we're operating on the in memory page as we're traversing an insert list and calling {{\_\_wt_txn_read_upd_list_}}. However as soon as the page gets evicted and some updates are written out to disk this process becomes more complicated calling: {{\_\_wt_txn_read_}} which subsequently calls {{\_\_wt_hs_find_upd_}} however it only calls {{\_\_wt_hs_find_upd}} if the thread that is searching for the prefix started prior to the thread that inserted and removed the prefix.

So there's a few potential workarounds here that I am currently investigating however neither are particularly nice:
 # We could in theory detect that the insertion and removal is happening in the same txn and modify the time window to go from 0->stop_txn. As the start_txn is 0 we wouldn't search the history store. However this would then make updates that previously weren't visible visible to older readers. As such this isn't a real solution but I have implemented a patch with this solution and it does resolve 90% of the regression.
 # If we prepend the prefixes with some kind of junk data or put them in a different table in theory we wouldn't run into this problem of search nearing for the prefix (when looking for the actual key) and iterating a large quantity of prefix updates.

I'm going to continue looking into this tomorrow and have a few patches in mind.

I am also planning on running this workload while fast pathing the history store lookup, to see how much deviation there is from 4.2 without any history store component. If I still see a large deviation then hopefully that will give me some clues as to where the search near logic has changed.
As a side note, as I'm sure its not clear from my lengthy posts there aren't any history store specific issues here. The search into the history store is still valid.

I'll try and give a full overview of this problem, why it works better in 4.2, worse in 4.4 and the solution in this post.

*Background:*

*Unique index insertions:*

A unique index *key* has the format {{(value, docid)}}, which at face value is a bit odd as only interested in in the {{value}} that is being inserted being unique. Why do we insert keys of this format then? There are scenarios that can lead to there being duplicate entries in a unique index, I'm not going to go into those here. Because we have this key format we have to insert keys into a unique index in a somewhat weird sequence of steps:

1. Insert the prefix key, prefix key = {{value}}
 2. Remove the prefix key
 3. Search near for the prefix key, this is called by {{_keyExists:wiredtiger_index.cpp}}
 4. Insert the unique index full key, i.e. {{(value, docid)}}

All 4 steps are wrapped in the same transaction. The insertion and removal of the prefix is done to guarantee that concurrent insertions by different threads conflict with our currently running transaction. As they too will attempt to insert the same prefix and be returned a write conflict. Wiredtiger has an API call that could in theory avoid the insertion and then removal, i.e. {{cursor->reserve()}} however that doesn't work in this scenario. This can be explained with the following example:

We have two threads T1, and T2. T1 starts before T2 and both are attempting to insert the value/prefix {{AAAA}}. Suppose for some reason T1 lags behind and T2 gets to insert and remove {{AAAA}} prior to T1. At this point T2 inserts the full key {{(AAAA, docid_T2)}} and commits, now had we used {{cursor->reserve()}} T1 would be able to come along and insert {{AAAA}} as well and not receive a conflict T1 would then search near, not see the full key inserted by T2 because its in the future and insert it's own {{(AAAA, docid_T1)}} violating the uniqueness of the index. As such the prefix itself needs to live in the table beyond the lifetime of T2's transaction. It won't be able to get cleaned up by garbage collection until after T1 finishes.

Next we do a search near for the prefix to validate whether someone had inserted a key of value {{(AAAA, docid_X)}} already, if this returns true we can detect that we've run into a duplicate key in our index and exit out. Given our above scenario this can be explained by saying a transaction T3 comes along after T1 and T2 have exited, it is also looking to add the value of {{AAAA}} to our unique index. It successfully insert / removes {{AAAA}} as a prefix, however when it search nears for {{AAAA}} it will find the {{(AAAA, docid_T2)}} and return that it has found a duplicate.

*Search near:*

This will become important later but is a bit of background knowledge, search near attempts to return the record itself if its a direct match or the logically adjacent record, which is either the smallest record larger than the key or the largest record smaller than the key. Which sounds reasonable but gets a bit sub optimal in an example scenario:

Suppose you have a table filled with keys {{a-z}}, key {{a}} was inserted with txn_id 1. The rest of the key range has txnid 5. And our currently running txn has txn id 3. Our txn does a search_near for key {{l}}, internally we're now in {{wt_btcur_search_near}} and we end up on key {{l}} which isn't visible to us so we cannot return it. To uphold the contract internally WiredTiger will call {{cursor_row_next}} to the end of the table, then {{cursor_row_prev}} to the other end and return a cursor pointing to key {{a}}.

*The problem:*

Inserting a large number of entries into a unique index with multiple concurrent threads results in one of the threads stalling and getting stuck looking for content in {{search_near}}. But only really causes a problem once the page/s being searched get evicted. The eviction piece here is interesting as it highlighted the difference between 4.2. and 4.4.

Prior to eviction all updates are going to be on update chains contained within insert lists in memory, which can be read quickly and the logic of reading these things doesn't differ much between 4.2 and 4.4.

*Why is 4.2 faster?*
 4.2 guarantees that the ondisk value must be globally visible, so the in memory pages cannot be evicted while we have an older reader/writer. In the scenario of our reproducer doing a lot of {{search_nears}} all the relevant pages it searches never leave memory, and we don't see a slowdown.

*Why is 4.4 slower?* 
 The eviction logic changed significantly in durable history, the on disk value isn't guaranteed to be visible and the page can be evicted as long as there exists some committed updates on it, so our update chain / insert lists can be removed from memory. The read logic also changed, now whenever we find an on disk value we need to look in the history store when we see it. But because the page is evicted which it isn't in 4.2 we're doing these reads on disk which is significantly slower.

*The solution:*
 The {{search_near}} performed by {{_keyExists}} is only interested in keys that contain the prefix in the table. However because of {{search_near's}} guarantee we traverse well outside of the prefix key_range, e.g. we're looking for {{AAAA}} and traverse all the way to {{ZZZZ}} just to return {{WT_NOTFOUND}}. We can add a config option to {{search_near}}, {{"prefix_search=true"}} which will exit the {{search_near}} call as soon as the key it's iterating over are outside of the prefix range. This will allow us to early exit our {{search_near}} and should reduce the impact of the pages getting evicted.

Thanks for the detailed explanation, [~luke.pearson]. 

Your proposed solution might also solve another problem we have with search_near on indexes with prepared updates: SERVER-41977. In indexes, if we search for a key prefix A, search_near may return a prefix for a different key, B. If B is involved in a prepared transaction, the cursor will block until that operation commits. It sounds like the "prefix_search=true" configuration could allow the cursor to return WT_NOTFOUND before landing on an unrelated key that might be involved in a prepared transaction. What do you think?
That does sound like similar problem and could be solved using this logic, do you have a basic reproducer I could run to test with? I should have a fix implemented after this week.

It appears that the issue also impacts TPC-C benchmark itself, not just data loading (when it happened during data loading) - BF-20413

The impact is smaller, but 'ss wt cache history table reads missed'  jump even higher than during data loading.

[~alex.podelko] have you looked into why those reads are missed, the scenario here involves a specific search near case that can be optimised. {{ss wt cache history table reads missed}} being a symptom, not the cause.

[~luke.pearson] It is intermittent - same as with data load - so my first guess was that it has the same root cause as for data load - the one you are investigating here. If you want me to look deeper into it - I will be happy to do so - but probably need some guidance from you what/how I should look into.

Does the TPCC loader create indexes, if so what kind? And I assume it's loading with N threads concurrently? If we had a call stack of where the history store reads were originating from we could at least identify which search near (if any) is causing the missed reads, then we could determine whether that one could be optimised or not.

I had a bit of free time to work on this, my initial implementation of the prefix search configuration does appear to resolve the problem.

Running the longer version of the reproducer with my changes:

real 0m8.707s
 user 0m25.281s
 sys 0m0.768s

Running 4.2:

real 0m7.919s
 user 0m24.852s
 sys 0m0.689s

There's still work to do here, mainly correctness testing and code layering issues, but it's looking promising. I'm interested in knowing if we can solve that prepared issue that was mentioned by [~louis.williams].

My understanding is that this change will also solve that issue [~louis.williams] mentioned. I don't think any special handling is required in the current algo to handle that case as well. The current solution will solve that as well, with the assumption that the prefix of the prepared update is different from the searched one, since WT_NOTFOUND will be returned from search_near when the searched prefix is not present.

I spent the day resolving a db_test failure that came about from cursor reusage and myself not correctly clearing the flag related to the prefix search, however involved a medium dive into how the validation stuff works.

Having fixed that failure I kicked off another patch build, and have a small but non-zero amount of red to take a look at, I'll begin looking into that this afternoon, hopefully have it resolved by sometime tomorrow. Before creating a final changeset for PR.

[~luke.pearson] that test is mostly a characterization of the resources consumed by the server because any unexpected changes would directly affect customer billing. However, the billing model has yet to be released, so as long as the changes in metrics make sense (i.e. fewer cursor seeks, or less data read by WT), feel free to modify the test.

So the above test failures can be attributed to the early exit of the {{_keyExists}} function. Essentially with the prefix search near fast path we don't return a value and as such we never perform a {{getKey}} call, this {{getKey}} call is what would increment our {{idxEntriesRead}} by 6.

As [~louis.williams] correctly suggested this isn't an issue with the code but rather a test that will need to be updated when the server portion of this change is completed. I suspect we'll have to merge the WiredTiger change, and quickly merge the SERVER change to avoid too many failures on the evergreen waterfall.

We could do something a bit better, such as disabling the test in a commit just prior to the merge, and then re-enabling with a fix afterwards.  Or we could commit the fix to the test in the same commit as the merge, if possible.
Oh right yeah we just merge the WiredTiger change and then merge the server change with the test fix included.

I've been working on a validating some potential scenarios where the prefix search code will cause us to miss seeing keys, essentially the prefix search is heavily reliant on the guarantee that {{__cursor_row_search}} will place us on the expected key range.

Suppose we have a set of keys:
 {{(aa, ab, ac, ba, bb, bc, ca, cb, cc)}}
 Now if I was to do a {{__cursor_row_search}} for a partial key {{a}} I must be guaranteed to place on {{(aa, ab, ac)}} or this code will exit and we'll never see our key range.

Additionally if we have the key set:
 {{(a, ai, b, bi, c, ci)}}
 However the updates associated with the prefix records are not visible to us, in other words we shouldn't be able to see {{(a, b, c)}}. Then we do a search_near for {{b}}, would the underlying {{__cursor_row_search}} guarantee that it lands on {{b}}? The answer appears to be also yes to this concern. {{__cursor_row_search}} doesn't pay attention to visibility when deciding which update to land on.

Furthermore there is one scenario that I think can't happen but if it did would again result in us not seeing keys, if we had the key set {{(a, b, c, cc, z)}} and {{cc}} isn't visible to us, we do an initial {{__cursor_row_search}} and land on {{cc}} (I believe this isn't possible and we land on {{c}}, but lets assume we land on {{cc}}. Now we can't see this key so we do a {{cursor->next}} and we're now on {{z}}, during this time someone inserts a key {{k}} between {{cc}} and {{z}} and because we've reached the end of the {{cursor->next}} traversal we do a {{cursor->prev}}, we see key {{k}} and exit due to prefix searching, missing key {{c}} which should've been returned.

bq. we see key k and exit due to prefix searching, missing key c which should've been returned.

There is a loop in the search_near post search traversals to handle this scenario. It keeps going until the found key matches the expected greater than or less than condition.

The PR for this work is in final review, so it should be merged soon. There's been a few mentions of potential improvements else where in the code base using this functionality however I would caution against using it without understanding the guarantees required for it to work as expected. If used improperly it may result in not seeing key/value pairs that should've been returned by a search near.

That main requirement here is that the underlying {{cursor_row_search}} will land on a key associated with the prefix key range, if in any other situation that cannot be guaranteed then please do not use the prefix key functionality. Unique index insertions of course guarantee that a key associated with the prefix key range must exist.

Author:{'name': 'Luke Pearson', 'email': 'luke.pearson@mongodb.com', 'username': 'luke-pearson'}
Message: WT-7264 Creating a new configuration for search near that allows it to exit quickly when searching for prefixes. (#6473)

* The new option modifies __wt_lex_compare to compare the prefix, which is the key set by the user prior to the search_near API call, with the tree_item up to the shortest length. The loops inside bt_curnext and bt_curprev have both had early escapes added, once we detect a key outside of range we return WT_NOTFOUND. The bt_cursor.c search_near loop will reset the cursor for us when we return WT_NOTFOUND so as to not leave the cursor positioned.
* The new API config can only be used for row store tables and cannot be used when a custom collator is defined. Two new error messages have been added for both of these scenarios.
* When cursor->reconfigure is called a CURSTD flag is set on the cursor to define it as a prefix search cursor.
Branch: develop
